headline: Vaughan home values are still drifting down: a typical home is about 5% cheaper than a year ago and about 30% below its 2022 peak. Fewer new projects are starting, and borrowing got slightly more expensive in October, but governments are cutting fees and taxes on new homes to restart building.

status.label: Fewer new homes starting
status.explanation: Vaughan started 968 homes in 2025, the fewest in the last ten years. Homes under construction fell to 3,144 in September 2026, from 3,588 a year earlier and a peak of 9,815.

status.label: Values still slipping
status.explanation: The typical Vaughan condo apartment is valued at $504,900, down 6.5% from a year ago and well below the $864,400 peak in March 2022.

status.label: Rents levelling off
status.explanation: Average rent in purpose-built rentals in the Richmond Hill/Vaughan/King area was $1,726 in 2025, slightly below $1,762 in 2024. Across Canada, asking rents in October 2026 were 3.2% lower than a year earlier.

status.label: Investors back, buyers cautious
status.explanation: New condo sales across the GTA and Hamilton doubled in mid-2026, helped by large bulk purchases. But the Bank of Canada raised rates in October and Ontario's unemployment rate reached 7.0%.

status.label: Policy pushing, economy pulling
status.explanation: Vaughan cut its development charges to zero for eligible projects and Ontario offers a full HST rebate on new homes up to $1 million. Higher rates and job losses push the other way.

personas.bottom_line: Prices are well below their peak and new homes come with large tax rebates, but borrowing just became a little more expensive.

points.text: A typical Vaughan condo apartment is valued at $504,900, down 6.5% in a year and about 42% below its 2022 peak of $864,400.
Ontario rebates the full 13% HST on new homes up to $1 million (up to $130,000) if you live in the home, and you don't have to be a first-time buyer.
On October 28, 2026 the Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5%, its first increase in more than three years. Mortgage rates tend to follow.
In October there were 4.8 months of homes for sale at the current pace of sales, and homes sold for about 97% of their asking price. That gives buyers more room to negotiate than in a hot market.

watch: Bank of Canada decision on December 9, 2026

personas.bottom_line: Rents in the Vaughan area have stopped rising, and lots of newly finished condos give renters more choice.

points.text: Average rent in purpose-built rentals in the Richmond Hill/Vaughan/King area was $1,726 in 2025, down from $1,762 in 2024. About 2.4% of units were empty.
Vaughan finished 6,368 new homes in 2025, the most in the last ten years. Many become rentals, which adds choice.
Across Canada, asking rents in October 2026 averaged $2,036, down 3.2% from a year earlier, though reports say Toronto rents have started rising again.
The CMHC numbers above cover purpose-built rental buildings only. Condo units rented by owners, which are common in the VMC, are not included.

watch: CMHC October 2026 rental survey (usually released in December)

personas.bottom_line: Family-sized homes cost less than at the peak, but few new ones are being started and most VMC homes are condo apartments.

points.text: A typical Vaughan townhouse is valued at $714,500, down 8.9% in a year. A typical detached house is $1,482,000.
Vaughan started only 968 homes of all kinds in 2025, so fewer new family homes are on the way.
The largest active VMC proposals are multi-tower plans, the biggest at about 4,563 units. This site can't yet tell how many of those units are family-sized.

watch: Number of 2- and 3-bedroom units in new VMC plans

personas.bottom_line: Compared with 2022 prices are much lower, but compared with ten years ago most owners are still ahead.

points.text: A typical Vaughan home is valued at $1,106,600, up about 23% from $896,000 ten years ago but about 30% below its March 2022 peak of $1,587,400.
For condo apartments, today's $504,900 compares with $420,300 ten years ago and $864,400 at the peak.
Sellers face competition: 1,219 homes were listed in October, about 4.8 months of supply at the current pace.
New condos can now come with an HST rebate of up to $130,000 for buyers who live in them, which makes new units more competitive with resale.

watch: Months of supply falling below about 4

personas.bottom_line: Lower prices help, but flat rents, many new completions and a rate hike make rental returns tight.

points.text: A typical Vaughan condo apartment is $504,900 while average purpose-built rent in the area is $1,726 a month. Condo rents can differ from this survey.
Large investors are buying again: GTA and Hamilton new condo sales doubled in the third quarter of 2026, helped by bulk purchases.
Ottawa plans to bring temporary residents down to 5% of the population by the end of 2027, which may mean fewer renters.
The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5% in October 2026, which raises borrowing costs.

personas.bottom_line: Moving from a detached house to a condo still frees up a large amount of money, a bit less than at the peak.

points.text: A typical detached house is valued at $1,482,000 and a typical condo apartment at $504,900, a gap of about $977,000.
At their 2022 peaks the gap was about $1,062,000 ($1,926,600 versus $864,400).
A new condo you live in can qualify for Ontario's full HST rebate if it costs up to $1 million.

watch: Gap between detached and condo values

scenarios.name: base
scenarios.summary: Prices stay flat or drift a little lower while the many recently finished condos are absorbed. Construction stays slow but stops falling as fee cuts and tax rebates help some projects start.

assumptions.assumption: Targets of 380,000 new permanent and 370,000 new temporary residents a year hold for 2027-2029
Zero city charges stay in place for projects starting by October 31, 2027

drivers.text: Zero city development charges and the new-home HST rebate lower the cost of building and buying new.
A record wave of completions in 2025 means many units are competing for buyers and renters.
Bulk purchases are lifting new condo sales from very low levels.

scenarios.name: optimistic
scenarios.summary: Rates ease again, jobs recover and builders rush to start projects before the fee and tax breaks expire. Prices stabilise and construction picks up.

assumptions.assumption: No further hikes, and back to 2.25% by the end of 2027
Several VMC towers start construction before the October 31, 2027 development-charge deadline

drivers.text: Lower borrowing costs bring buyers back.
Fee cuts and rebates have a deadline, which encourages builders to start soon.

scenarios.name: pessimistic
scenarios.summary: More rate hikes and job losses, plus fewer newcomers, push prices and rents lower and keep new construction near its lows.

assumptions.assumption: Rises to 3.0% or higher by mid-2027
Temporary residents fall to 5% of the population by the end of 2027 as planned, reducing rental demand

drivers.text: Higher rates make mortgages and investor loans more expensive.
Very few new condo projects launched in early 2026, so fewer towers can start later.

baseline_views.reason: Values have fallen 5.5% in a year and there are 4.8 months of supply, so a further small decline is likely. The October rate hike adds pressure, but it is small.
Weak jobs and possible further rate hikes weigh on prices. Cheaper new homes (HST rebate) compete with resale. Nothing strong enough to move far from the baseline.
The baseline assumes no change, but condo values fell 6.5% last year and the 2025 wave of completions is still being absorbed.
Plans to cut temporary residents may reduce rental demand, and new condos with HST rebates compete with resale units.
Zero city development charges and the HST rebate encourage starts, but projects need pre-sales and new launches were very low in early 2026.
Same forces as total starts. One or two towers starting or not can swing the total a lot.
Completions have been running far above starts (6,368 finished versus 968 started in 2025), so the number under construction should keep shrinking.
Asking rents fell nationally but are steadying in Toronto. Survey averages include long-term tenants and move slowly.

events.title: Bank of Canada raises its rate to 2.5%
events.impact: The first increase in more than three years. Mortgages and investor loans cost a little more.

events.title: Next Bank of Canada rate decision
events.impact: Markets are split on whether another hike comes in December or January.

events.title: 2027-2029 immigration plan keeps targets flat
events.impact: 380,000 new permanent and 370,000 new temporary residents a year, with a goal of cutting temporary residents to 5% of the population by the end of 2027. Steady but slower population growth means less new rental demand.

events.title: Canada loses 68,000 jobs in September
events.impact: Ontario's unemployment rate reached 7.0%, the highest among large provinces. Job worries keep buyers cautious.

events.title: Bulk buyers lift GTA new condo sales
events.impact: New condo sales rose from very low levels, but reports warn the pipeline of future projects is drying up.

events.title: Ontario's Bill 98 becomes law
events.impact: Aims to speed up planning approvals and lower building costs.

events.title: Vaughan cuts its development charges to zero
events.impact: Eligible residential projects that start construction between February 25, 2026 and October 31, 2027 pay no city development charges, which can make VMC towers cheaper to build.

events.title: Full HST rebate on new homes up to $1 million
events.impact: Up to $130,000 back for people buying a new home to live in, which helps new condo sales.

watch_list.threshold: Another hike on December 9, 2026 or in January
watch_list.why: Each increase makes mortgages and investor loans more expensive.

watch_list.threshold: Two months in a row of increases
watch_list.why: That would suggest prices have stopped falling.

watch_list.threshold: Below 3 favours sellers; above 5 favours buyers
watch_list.why: Shows who has the upper hand in negotiations.
Would show the development-charge cut is getting towers started.

watch_list.signal: Rental vacancy in the Vaughan area
watch_list.why: Would mean renters have more bargaining power and rents may fall.
Rising job losses would weaken demand for homes.
